title: DFS on Rome: Real Street Intersections ⚡
description: Watch Depth First Search (DFS) explore Trastevere’s street intersections like a real routing map—one branch deep at a time. You’ll see how graph traversal order changes the path, the stack behavior, and why DFS can “miss” the fastest route.
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps — what happens when DFS explores city intersections ⚡

In this visualization, each street intersection is a node and each road segment is an edge (a graph). DFS uses a stack/recursion to go as deep as possible before backtracking—so the *exploration order* is everything.

🔍 Key mechanics (DFS explained):
• LIFO behavior: DFS dives down one route until it hits a dead end.
• Backtracking: when a node has no unvisited neighbors, it pops back to try alternatives.
• Visited set: prevents infinite loops on cyclic street graphs.

✅ Takeaway: DFS guarantees *a traversal*, but not the shortest path—unless you’re lucky with the map order.

🤔 Debate question: If we randomize neighbor ordering on the same street graph, will DFS find the “better-looking” path more often—or just a different path every time?
